summary:
Point A is closed and is not a decision. Point B is a real choice: one open decision, D-PRE-52. The id D-PRE-51 stays free.

Files, all below /Users/diegohaz/.claude/jobs/f65a6229/tmp/round7/decisions/two-points:
- decisions.json: one decision, D-PRE-52, in the form of content/decisions.json.
- fragments/D-PRE-52.html: evidence, one compare demo, and the placeholder.
- fragments/CLOSED-run-approval-large.html: optional record text for point A, with no panel.
- closed.md: how the record closes point A, and what the implementation must do. One short part for point B.
- notes.md: how each fact was verified, the alternatives, the checks, and 9 doubts.
- evidence/ (7 Cloudflare pages, 2 lab probe results), scripts/, and check/ (a draft build with 59 decisions).

Checks: the draft build passes (apps/lab/audit/build.mjs with --content and --out), and check.mjs passes each check at 1440 px and at 400 px. 34 cited lines hold the cited words. No file of the worktree changed, no commit, no request to production.

POINT A (run approval of a large run): closed.
- Counted from code: today no page sends more than one screenshot in a command. The route accepts a list in a 1 MiB body (apps/web/src/api/review.ts:842, :847-851). A batch that D1 refuses is tried up to 5 times (apps/web/src/operations/review-queue.ts:62, :147-156; packages/service/src/work.ts:185-207), and then the page gets HTTP 409 with the code "conflict" (review.ts:812-830).
- Measured (document read, https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/platform/limits/, last change 2026-04-21): 30 seconds for a query, and "this duration limit also applies to the entire batch call". "A single query that attempts to modify hundreds of thousands of rows or hundreds of MBs of data at once will exceed execution limits." One database "processes queries one at a time". No count of rows or statements for one batch. A batch rolls back as a whole (https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/worker-api/d1-database/#batch).
- Calculation from values that the audit measured on a local D1 (5 rows for each change and 8; 4 of them in one INSERT; 1,929 bytes for a decision row): 20,000 changes are 100,008 rows, with 80,000 rows and 38.6 MB in the largest statement. The lowest count that the D1 words can mean is 25,000 changes (100,000 rows in one statement). "Hundreds of MBs" starts at about 51,800 changes.
- Reach: today a run has at most about 4,750 changes (from the record). After step 1 of D-DATA-02 it has at most about 20,000, which is below the words about rows and megabytes. After step 2 the count is reachable. The 30 seconds are not known for production.
- Why no choice: "save nothing" is what a transaction does. Parts are the option of D-SCALE-02 that the maintainer did not select, and they change "in one transaction" and "one Undo" of D-WORK-04. A button that is off above a count is the limit of D-SCALE-02, which is deferred and needs a production measurement. From the record: the closed summary of today writes 8 rows for each change, more than the run approval, so a guard for the button alone does not answer a mass change.

POINT B (the variant that a screenshot opens on): decision D-PRE-52, three options, option 1 recommended.
- Measured in the lab (Chromium 153, scenarios changes and one-browser): a row click, Up and Down, and a return after a decision all open the first variant that needs review. No memory. Example: on ariakit-ui-button/page/default the reviewer goes to Firefox, Light, presses Down and Up, and sees Chromium, Light again.
- Counted from code: the app of today has two rules. A row link opens the first variant that needs review (apps/web/src/review/review-workspace.tsx:457). Up and Down open the remembered variant (:355-368). Both come from pull request #104 of the maintainer (commit 859ad6f, 2026-09-27), and tests pin both.
- Counted: the saved rules say a third thing. D04 selected "Remember the last variant for each item", and line 271 of docs/simplification-audit/contract-issue-1.md and line 82 of docs/review-guide.md add "First visit uses its first variant".
- Counted: none of the 30 lab decisions names this rule (apps/lab/src/lab/record.ts:38-88), and no D-WORK answer does. So the lab page conflicts with an explicit earlier choice, and the record asks.

decisions.question: When you go to another screenshot, which of its variants does the review page show first?
decisions.options: 1. first-to-review: one rule and no memory. A row click, Up and Down, and a link with no variant open the first variant that needs review, then the first variant with a change, then the first variant. It is the lab page as it is, so the move adds no code. It changes the earlier decision D04, line 271 of the saved issue #1 text, and line 82 of the review guide. | 2. keys-remember: two rules, as the app of today. A row click opens the first variant that needs review. Up and Down open the variant that the reviewer selected last in that screenshot. About 20 lines and 2 tests (estimate). The reviewer can go between two screenshots and keep a variant in each, but the keys can open an approved or unchanged variant while another one needs review. D04 and pull request #104 stay. | 3. all-paths-remember: one rule with memory on each path, which the finding WORK-32 recommended. It takes back the row link rule of pull request #104, and the record of that pull request declined it on 2026-09-27. Not in the panel, with a reason in the rationale and in notes.md: always the first variant (it opens an unchanged variant on each of 12 screenshots in the lab scenario one-browser), and the variant with the same key as before (not selected in D04).
decisions.recommended: Option 1, first-to-review. Reasons: one rule in place of two (standing rule 3), it is the lab page that the maintainer picked so the move adds no code, and each path opens a variant that needs review, which is the reason that pull request #104 gave for row links. The recommendation is wrong if the maintainer uses Up and Down to go between two screenshots and compare one variant of each: then option 2. It is also weaker if his lab note "remember user selection between items, variants, and even runs" meant the variant and not only the view of the stage.

closed: Point A, the run approval of a large run: closed by D-WORK-04 ("in one transaction", "one Undo reverses the command"), by D-SCALE-02 (a stated limit of changed captures, nothing built now, parts not selected), and by the D1 rule that a batch rolls back as a whole. Words of the maintainer: "Let's defer this to when this is a problem." Details: /Users/diegohaz/.claude/jobs/f65a6229/tmp/round7/decisions/two-points/closed.md, parts A1 to A6.

Point A, what the implementation must do in step 3 of the issue review-decisions: (1) keep one D1 batch, so a refused approval saves no decision row; (2) do not try a refused run approval again, because the queue of today tries 5 times and each try can hold the single-threaded database for up to 30 seconds; (3) answer with an own error code, not "conflict" (proposal: run_approval_too_large); (4) print a status line text that says nothing was saved and that the way forward is one screenshot at a time; (5) the same for the Undo of a run approval (measured on a local D1 by the audit: 11,505 rows for 3,832 targets); (6) keep the event visible to the operator; (7) one test for the single attempt. It must not build a limit of changes, a button that is off above a count, a state "approval in progress", or a test write to production D1.

Point A, when it opens again (a reading of this part, not a text of the record): at the first refusal of a run approval in production, or with the pull request that raises the capture limit of one run above about 20,000 (step 2 of D-DATA-02), which makes 25,000 changes possible.

doubts: Point A: the closure holds for the D1 words about rows and megabytes, not for the 30 seconds of one batch. Nobody measured a time on production D1. The audit measured 0.9 s and 16 s for 30,000 changes on a local D1, and the slow run was on a loaded computer. If production is about 3 times slower than that run, a run approval of 20,000 changes fails. The own error code is what makes this visible.

Point A: "one try" for a run approval is a reading of this part. The settled answer to D-RES-06 says that the server "tries a stored decision again by itself". Another form is possible: try again only for the errors that the D1 error list marks with "Retry the operation". If the maintainer wants the same count of tries for each stored command, item 2 of closed.md is wrong.
Point A: the two events that open the point again are not in the record. A note of the maintainer can correct them.
Point A: this part did not run a D1 probe again. The rows and the bytes for each change come from the saved probe results of the audit (rounds 2 and 4), which its checker ran a second time.
Point A: the code name run_approval_too_large and the status line text are proposals.

Point B: the maintainer selected the memory two times (D04, and pull request #104 for the keys), and the recommendation goes against that. It rests on standing rule 3 and on the lab page. His lab note "remember user selection between items, variants, and even runs" is read by the lab as the view of the stage (apps/lab/docs/design/round-2.md:60). If he meant the variant too, option 2 is nearer to his words.

Point B: one reading closes it with no panel: D-WORK-03 keeps the keys and the contract keeps D04, so the lab page has a defect and the new page must get the memory. This part did not take that reading, because the maintainer picked the lab page as it is and rule 3 prefers its one rule.

Point B: the app of today was read in its code and its tests, and not driven. The example of the panel uses the lab fixture for each option. "About 20 lines" is a count of the app lines that hold the memory, not of new code.

Both points: revision r8 was in work in the worktree. This part used the stable r7 copy of the section file. The file 60-workspace-viewer.html of the worktree was byte for byte equal to its r7 copy when this part compared them.
